title: The White House Menagerie
subtitle: The Roosevelt Pets
intro: A badger named after the boy who caught it. A snake named after a thin aunt. A pony that took the passenger lift to the second floor. Staff at the White House between 1901 and 1909 described the place as under occupation. Twelve questions on the Roosevelt animals.
heroAlt: Archie Roosevelt with Josiah, his pet badger
heroCredit: Archie and Josiah, his pet badger. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Archie Roosevelt kept a pet badger. What was it called?
questions.explanation: Josiah — named not for a president or a poet but for the boy who caught him. A little girl came up to Roosevelt on a train platform and asked whether he would like a baby badger her brother Josiah had just found. He would.
questions.imageAlt: Archie Roosevelt holding Josiah the badger
questions.credit: Archie and Josiah, his pet badger. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How did Archie's pony get up to the second floor of the White House?
options: It was carried up the service stairs
It never did — the story is a myth
It was hoisted through a window
questions.explanation: Seven-year-old Archie was ill upstairs, so his brothers coaxed the pony into the passenger elevator and took it to his bedroom to cheer him up. Tad Lincoln had once brought a goat into the White House. The Roosevelt boys went one better.
questions.imageAlt: Quentin Roosevelt on a pony beside a White House policeman
questions.credit: Quentin Roosevelt on pony beside White House policeman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Alice Roosevelt carried a green snake in her handbag. What was it called?
questions.explanation: Emily Spinach — Emily for an aunt Alice considered notably thin, and Spinach for the colour. She took it to parties. It is difficult to think of a detail that captures Alice better.
questions.imageAlt: Mr. and Mrs. Theodore Roosevelt with their children and a dog
questions.credit: Mr. and Mrs. Theodore Roosevelt with children and dog. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What was unusual about Slippers, one of the White House cats?
options: He was said to be able to open doors on his own
questions.explanation: A grey cat with six toes, and enough standing in the household that he is remembered by name alongside Tom Quartz, the other Roosevelt cat.
questions.imageAlt: The Roosevelt family with a dog
questions.credit: Mr. and Mrs. Theodore Roosevelt with children and dog. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Pete, a bull terrier, was removed from the White House. Why?
options: He belonged to a departing staff member
He was frightened of the cats
questions.explanation: Pete bit so many callers that the president reluctantly exiled him to Oyster Bay. Reports at the time included a French ambassador's trousers. Even Roosevelt, who tolerated a great deal from his animals, had a limit.
questions.imageAlt: Kermit Roosevelt with his dog Jack
questions.credit: Kermit Roosevelt and his dog Jack. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: The children kept a young bear. What did they name it?
options: Cotton Mather, after the Puritan divine
Bruin, out of the old storybooks
questions.explanation: Jonathan Edwards, after the eighteenth-century preacher of hellfire sermons — a joke about the animal's temperament that tells you something about the reading level in that nursery. Sources differ on whether he was a black bear or a cinnamon; they agree he was untamable.
questions.imageAlt: Josiah the badger with Archie at Sagamore Hill
questions.credit: Josiah and his master (Archie) at Sagamore, about 1905. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Eli Yale was which sort of animal?
questions.explanation: A blue macaw belonging to Ted, named with the cheerful disrespect of a Harvard family. He lived upstairs and was, by most accounts, loud.
questions.imageAlt: Kermit Roosevelt with his dog Jack
questions.credit: Kermit Roosevelt and his dog Jack. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What did Kermit bring to the breakfast table in his pocket?
questions.explanation: A kangaroo rat, regularly. Kermit was the quietest of the boys and in some ways the strangest — he later went with his father to Africa and down an uncharted river in the Amazon, so the small mammal at breakfast was an early sign.
questions.imageAlt: Kermit Roosevelt with his dog Jack
questions.credit: Kermit Roosevelt and his dog Jack. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Where were guests most likely to find a live reptile?
questions.explanation: The children hid live reptiles in sofa cushions, walked upstairs on stilts, and waded in the fountains on the grounds. The Roosevelt White House was not a quiet building and nobody involved pretended otherwise.
questions.imageAlt: The Roosevelt family with a dog
questions.credit: Mr. and Mrs. Theodore Roosevelt with children and dog. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Which of these was NOT among the Roosevelt animals?
questions.explanation: No tiger. The list is strange enough without one: a badger, macaws, a bear, snakes, guinea pigs, a one-legged rooster, a barn owl, an eagle, a coyote, dogs, cats and ponies. Foreign heads of state sent animals, and the children kept them.
questions.imageAlt: Archie Roosevelt with Josiah the badger
questions.credit: Archie and Josiah, his pet badger. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt's interest in animals began long before the White House. How early?
options: In the Badlands, when he took up ranching
At Harvard, in the natural history courses
As a boy, with a museum in his bedroom
Only once he had children of his own
questions.explanation: He founded the grandly named Roosevelt Museum of Natural History as a child — a collection of skins, nests, mounted birds and pickled specimens that began in his own bedroom and had to be moved out of it as it grew. He learned taxidermy from a man who had travelled with Audubon, and published an ornithological catalogue at eighteen. The White House menagerie was a family tradition with a long start.
questions.imageAlt: Josiah the badger at Sagamore Hill
questions.credit: Josiah and his master (Archie) at Sagamore, about 1905. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What happened to the animals when the Roosevelts left the White House in 1909?
options: They were released into the countryside
They were sold at auction with the stable stock
They were left behind for the Taft children
questions.explanation: The whole household moved with the family. Sagamore Hill had been their home since 1885 and had always kept animals — the menagerie simply went back to Oyster Bay, where Pete the bull terrier had already been sent ahead in disgrace. Roosevelt lived there until he died in 1919.

questions.credit: Mr. and Mrs. Theodore Roosevelt with children and dog. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.
